claim: CTCF and cohesin are key drivers of 3D-nuclear organization, anchoring the megabase-scale Topologically Associating Domains (TADs) that segment the genome.
source: CTCF and cohesin are key drivers of 3D-nuclear organization, anchoring the megabase-scale Topologically Associating Domains (TADs) that segment the genome.
evidence: This is a statement of established scientific knowledge about CTCF and cohesin's role in genome organization, supported by citations in the introduction.

claim: Intra-TAD loop anchors are structurally indistinguishable from TAD anchors regarding binding partners, sequence conservation, and resistance to cohesin knockdown.
source: The intra-TAD loop anchors identified are structurally indistinguishable from TAD anchors regarding binding partners, sequence conservation, and resistance to cohesin knockdown
evidence: This claim is supported by data presented in Figure 2 showing comparisons between TAD and intra-TAD loop anchors across multiple structural features.

claim: Intra-TAD loops retain key functional features of TADs, including chromatin contact insulation, blockage of repressive histone mark spread, and ubiquity across tissues.
source: further, the intra-TAD loops retain key functional features of TADs, including chromatin contact insulation, blockage of repressive histone mark spread, and ubiquity across tissues.
evidence: This claim is supported by data in Figure 3 showing insulation properties and Figure 2 showing tissue conservation.

claim: Intra-TAD loops form by the same loop extrusion mechanism as the larger TAD loops.
source: We propose that intra-TAD loops form by the same loop extrusion mechanism as the larger TAD loops
evidence: This is a proposed mechanism based on inference from the structural similarities between intra-TAD loops and TADs.

claim: The shorter length of intra-TAD loops enables finer regulatory control in restricting enhancer-promoter interactions.
source: their shorter length enables finer regulatory control in restricting enhancer-promoter interactions, which enables selective, high-level expression of gene targets of super-enhancers and genes located within repressive nuclear compartments.
evidence: This claim is supported by data showing gene expression patterns within intra-TAD loops and their relationship to enhancers.

claim: TADs are insulated chromatin domains averaging ~700 kb in length.
source: The mammalian genome is organized into stereotypical domains, averaging ~700 kb in length, called Topologically Associating Domains (TADs) (Dixon et al., 2012; Nora et al., 2012).
evidence: This is established knowledge from prior studies, supported by citations.

claim: TAD boundaries are often retained across tissues.
source: TADs are insulated chromatin domains whose genomic boundaries are often retained across tissues (Dixon et al., 2012)
evidence: This is established knowledge from prior studies, supported by citation.

claim: TAD boundaries have been conserved during mammalian evolution.
source: TADs are insulated chromatin domains whose genomic boundaries are often retained across tissues (Dixon et al., 2012) and have been conserved during mammalian evolution (Vietri Rudan et al., 2015; Dixon et al., 2015).
evidence: This is established knowledge from prior studies, supported by citations.

claim: Genomic regions co-bound by cohesin and CTCF (CAC sites) are strongly enriched at TAD boundaries.
source: Genomic regions co-bound by cohesin and CTCF (CAC sites) were strongly enriched at TAD boundaries (Figure 1A), consistent with (Vietri Rudan et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is directly supported by data shown in Figure 1A and is consistent with prior literature.

claim: Cohesin-non-CTCF sites (CNC sites) are weakly depleted at TAD boundaries.
source: In contrast, cohesin-non-CTCF sites (CNC sites) were weakly depleted at TAD boundaries.
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 1A.

claim: Strong enrichment for motif-oriented CTCF binding occurs at TAD boundaries.
source: We also observed strong enrichment for motif-oriented CTCF binding at TAD boundaries (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A), consistent with recent reports and the loop extrusion model of domain formation (Vietri Rudan et al., 2015; Sanborn et al., 2015; Rao et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by data in Figure 1—figure supplement 1A and is consistent with prior literature.

claim: Cohesin binding sites resistant to loss are enriched at TAD boundaries in both hepatocytes and MEFs.
source: In both cell types, sites resistant to cohesin loss are enriched at TAD boundaries, while those sensitive to cohesin loss are more equally distributed along the TAD length.
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 1B comparing cohesin binding site distribution.

claim: CTCF sites shared across 12 or more tissues show 3-4 fold enrichment at TAD boundaries relative to the center of the TAD.
source: CTCF sites that are shared across 12 or more tissues showed 3–4 fold enrichment at TAD boundaries relative to the center of the TAD, whereas CTCF binding sites unique to liver, or shared with only one other tissue, showed no such enrichment (Figure 1C).
evidence: This claim is directly supported by data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: TAD boundaries are enriched for CpG hypomethylation, most pronounced at TAD anchor CTCF motifs.
source: TAD boundaries were also enriched for CpG hypomethylation, which was most pronounced at TAD anchor CTCF motifs (Figure 1D, Figure 1—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 1D and Figure 1—figure supplement 2A.

claim: TAD boundary enrichment seen for CTCF and cohesin is absent for >50 other liver-expressed TFs.
source: By comparison, the TAD boundary enrichment seen for CTCF and cohesin was absent for >50 other liver-expressed TFs whose binding site distribution within TADs we examined (Figure 1E, and data not shown).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 1E and additional unpublished data.

claim: 40.9% of liver TAD boundaries represent transitions from inactive to active chromatin compartments or vice versa.
source: A subset comprised of 1439 liver TAD boundaries (40.9% of all boundaries) represents transitions from inactive to active chromatin compartments, or vice versa (Figure 1F; 2nd and 3rd clusters).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 1F showing k-means clustering of TAD boundaries.

claim: Genes in active TADs show median liver expression of 1.095 FPKM compared to 0.003 FPKM for genes in inactive TADs.
source: Striking differences in gene expression were seen between active and inactive compartment TADs (median liver expression 1.095 FPKM for 12,258 genes in active TADs vs. 0.003 FPKM for 4643 genes in inactive TADs; Figure 1H).
evidence: This claim is directly supported by data shown in Figure 1H comparing gene expression between TAD types.

claim: A greater fraction of genes located in inactive TADs are tissue-specific compared to genes in active TADs.
source: A greater fraction of genes located in inactive TADs are tissue-specific compared to genes in active TADs (Figure 1I).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 1I showing Tau score distributions.

claim: Only 20.2% of all genes in inactive TADs are expressed in liver (FPKM >1) vs. 51.3% of genes in active TADs.
source: Overall, only 939 (20.2%) of all 4643 genes in inactive TADs are expressed in liver (FPKM >1) vs. 6,290 (51.3%) of the 12,258 genes in active TADs.
evidence: This claim is supported by analysis of gene expression data within different TAD types.

claim: Only 14.7% of liver CTCF binding sites are associated with TAD boundaries.
source: Overall, only 14.7% of liver CTCF binding sites are associated with TAD boundaries (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A), consistent with other reports (Dixon et al., 2012)
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1A and is consistent with prior literature.

claim: Only 23% of CTCF-bound regions that retain all four features (tissue ubiquitous, cohesin knockdown-resistant, species-conserved, and at TAD boundaries) are within 25 kb of a TAD boundary.
source: only 23% of the CTCF-bound regions that retain all four of the above features are within 25 kb of a TAD boundary (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1A.

claim: The computational method identified 9543 intra-TAD loops present in all four liver samples, with a median length of 151 kb.
source: Applying this algorithm to each of 4 matched pairs of liver ChIP datasets for CTCF and cohesin, we identified a set of 9543 intra-TAD loops present in all four liver samples, with a median length of 151 kb.
evidence: This claim describes the results of the computational method applied to the data.

claim: 91% of predicted intra-TAD loops are wholly contained within a single TAD, versus only 67% for a random shuffled control.
source: Moreover, 91% of our predicted intra-TAD loops were wholly contained within a single TAD, versus only 67% for a random shuffled control (Figure 2—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1E comparing predicted loops to random controls.

claim: 17.1% of intra-TAD loops share one CTCF loop anchor with a TAD boundary.
source: The final set of 9543 liver intra-TAD loops includes 1632 intra-TAD loops (17.1%) that share one CTCF loop anchor with a TAD boundary (i.e., an intra-TAD loop nested in a TAD with a potential shared anchor).
evidence: This claim describes a specific subset of the predicted intra-TAD loops.

claim: TAD and intra-TAD loop anchors are more tissue ubiquitous than other categories of CTCF/CAC sites.
source: Figure 2C shows the tissue distribution of CTCF binding at CTCF binding sites found at intra-TAD loop anchors in liver, where an x-axis value of 1 indicates the liver CTCF binding site is occupied by CTCF in only one other tissue, and a value of 15 indicates binding occurs in all 15 mouse tissues where CTCF ChIP-seq data is available. Results show that a large majority of intra-TAD loop anchors are bound by CTCF in at least 10 of the 15 mouse tissues examined.
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 2C comparing tissue conservation across CTCF site categories.

claim: 80% of TAD anchors and 90% of intra-TAD loop anchors are resistant to the loss of cohesin binding in Rad21+/- mice vs. only 52.8% for all CAC sites.
source: Further, we found that 80% of TAD anchors and 90% of intra-TAD loop anchors are resistant to the loss of cohesin binding in Rad21+/- mice vs. only 52.8% for all CAC sites (Figure 2D).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 2D comparing cohesin knockdown resistance.

claim: 70.6% of TAD anchors and 77.6% of intra-TAD loop anchors are comprised of 'triple sites' where cohesin and CTCF are co-bound with Top2b, vs. only 46.6% for all CTCF sites.
source: Moreover, a large fraction of TAD and intra-TAD loop anchors, 70.6% and 77.6%, respectively, are comprised of 'triple sites', where cohesin and CTCF are co-bound with Top2b, a potential component of the loop extrusion complex (Uusküla-Reimand et al., 2016), vs. only 46.6% for the set of all CTCF sites (Figure 2D).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 2D comparing Top2b co-binding.

claim: TAD and intra-TAD loop anchors show greater sequence conservation within the core 18 bp CTCF motif than other CTCF sites.
source: TAD and intra-TAD loop anchors show greater sequence conservation within the core 18 bp CTCF motif than other CTCF sites (Figure 2E).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 2E showing PhastCons conservation scores.

claim: 62-63% of intra-TAD loops predicted in liver overlap with loops identified experimentally by Hi-C in mESCs or NPCs.
source: Predicted loops were similar in number and size across cell types, with substantial overlap between intra-TAD loops predicted in liver compared to loops identified experimentally by Hi-C in mESCs or NPCs (62–63%; Figure 2—figure supplement 4A).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 4A comparing predicted loops to experimental Hi-C data.

claim: 57-63% of predicted intra-TAD loops overlap with CAC-anchored loops identified in mESC using ChIA-PET for Smc1.
source: We also observed 57–63% overlap of our predicted intra-TAD loops across the 3 cell types with CAC-anchored loops identified in mESC using ChIA-PET for the cohesin subunit Smc1 (Dowen et al., 2014; Handoko et al., 2011; Hnisz et al., 2016) (Figure 2B, Figure 2—figure supplement 4A).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 2B and Figure 2—figure supplement 4A comparing predicted loops to ChIA-PET data.

claim: The substantial overlap between intra-TAD loops across mouse cell types is very similar to the overlap between TADs.
source: The substantial overlap between intra-TAD loops across mouse cell types is very similar to the overlap between TADs, indicating a similar level of tissue ubiquity for intra-TAD loops as for TADs (Figure 2—figure supplement 4B).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 4B comparing tissue conservation.

claim: Loops predicted in multiple cell types had stronger interactions than tissue-specific or other loops, as determined by Smc1 ChIA-PET in mESC.
source: Further, loops that were predicted in multiple cell types had stronger interactions than tissue-specific or other loops, as determined by Smc1 ChIA-PET in mESC (Figure 2—figure supplement 4C).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 4C comparing interaction strengths.

claim: ~75% of intra-TAD loops identified in mouse liver are experimentally observed in at least one other cell type (mESCs, CH12, or mouse NPCs).
source: Overall, ~75% of intra-TAD loops that we identified in mouse liver are experimentally observed in at least one other cell type (mESCs, CH12, or mouse NPCs).
evidence: This claim summarizes the validation of predicted loops across multiple cell types.

claim: 48.5% (4,632) of computationally predicted liver intra-TAD loops are present in both mESCs and NPCs.
source: Further, 48.5% (4,632) of the computationally predicted liver intra-TAD loops were also present in both mESCs and NPCs (Supplementary file 1B).
evidence: This claim describes the overlap of predicted loops across three cell types.

claim: TAD and intra-TAD anchors both show strong directional interactions compared to non-anchor CTCF sites.
source: TAD and intra-TAD anchors both show strong directional interactions compared to non-anchor CTCF sites, and TAD anchors show stronger interactions than intra-TAD loop anchors.
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 3A comparing inward bias indices.

claim: For virtual 4C viewpoints placed downstream of a left intra-TAD loop anchor, interaction reads are shifted in favor of the downstream direction, comprising 58.8-79.9% of Hi-C read pairs.
source: For virtual 4C viewpoints placed downstream of a left intra-TAD loop anchor (i.e., within an intra-TAD loop; IN), interaction reads were shifted in favor of the downstream direction, which comprised 58.8–79.9% of the Hi-C read pairs.
evidence: This claim is supported by virtual 4C analysis shown in Figure 3B and Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: TAD and intra-TAD loop anchors show greater insulation of H3K27me3 and H3K9me3 repressive marks than other CTCF sites.
source: For H3K27me3 signal distribution, TAD and intra-TAD loop anchors showed the greatest insulation, but were not significantly different from each other (Kolmogorov-Smirnov (KS) test; p=0.52). The same general trend was observed for H3K9me3 signal insulation; however, intra-TAD loop anchors actually showed greater insulation than TAD anchors and all other groups (KS test; p<0.001).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 3D comparing JSD insulation scores.

claim: CNC sites consistently show the least insulation of both repressive histone marks.
source: CNC sites consistently showed the least insulation of both repressive histone marks, as expected.
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 3D comparing insulation across site types.

claim: ~70,000 mouse liver DNase hypersensitive sites (DHS) were identified and classified into five classes based on H3K4me1 and H3K4me3 ratios.
source: We previously identified ~70,000 mouse liver DNase hypersensitive sites (DHS), whose chromatin accessibility is in part determined by TF binding and their flanking histone marks (Sugathan and Waxman, 2013; Ling et al., 2010). To assign a function for each DHS, we classified each DHS according to the ratio of two chromatin marks, H3K4me1 and H3K4me3, which are respectively associated with enhancers and promoters (Wang et al., 2008). The ~70,000 DHS were grouped into five classes: promoter, weak promoter, enhancer, weak enhancer and insulator (Figure 4A, Figure 4—figure supplement 1A; see Materials and methods).
evidence: This claim describes the classification method for DHS regions based on histone mark ratios.

claim: Enhancer-DHS bind cohesin largely in the absence of CTCF, while promoter-DHS are bound by both CTCF and cohesin.
source: Using this simplified five DHS class model, we observed that enhancer-DHS bind cohesin largely in the absence of CTCF, while promoter-DHS are bound by both CTCF and cohesin (Figure 4B).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 4B showing binding patterns across DHS classes.

claim: 503 core super-enhancers were identified in mouse liver that show strong signal regardless of sex or time of day.
source: In total, we identified 503 core super-enhancers, that is, super-enhancers that show strong signal regardless of sex or time of day (Figure 4—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: This claim describes the identification of super-enhancers using the ROSE pipeline across multiple samples.

claim: Core super-enhancers represent 14.1% of all enhancer regions in the genome and 2.8% of all enhancer clusters.
source: Core super-enhancers represent 14.1% of all enhancer regions in the genome (6680 of 47,372 constituent enhancers + weak enhancers), and 2.8% of all enhancer clusters, defined as groups of enhancers within 12.5 kb of one another (503 of all 17,964 enhancer clusters).
evidence: This claim quantifies the proportion of super-enhancers relative to all enhancers.

claim: Both protein coding and lncRNA genes that neighbor super-enhancers are more highly expressed and tissue-specific compared to genes neighboring typical enhancers.
source: Both protein coding and lncRNA genes that neighbor super-enhancers are more highly expressed and tissue-specific when compared to all genes, or to all genes neighboring typical enhancers (KS test p-value<0.0001; Figure 4D).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 4D comparing gene expression and tissue specificity.

claim: Only 6.8% of genes proximal to liver super-enhancers are targets of super-enhancers in mESCs or pro-B cells.
source: Consistent with this tissue specificity, only 6.8% of genes proximal to liver super-enhancers are targets of super-enhancers in mESCs or pro-B cells (Figure 4E)
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 4E comparing super-enhancer targets across tissues.

claim: 55.2% of genes proximal to liver typical enhancers are proximal to typical enhancers in mESCs or pro-B cells.
source: whereas 55.2% of genes proximal to liver typical enhancers are proximal to typical enhancers in the other two cell types.
evidence: This claim is supported by comparison of typical enhancer targets across tissues.

claim: Super-enhancers show much greater accumulation of RNA polymerase 2 despite the lack of the promoter mark H3K4me3.
source: Super-enhancers showed much greater accumulation of RNA polymerase 2, despite the lack of the promoter mark H3K4me3 (Figure 4F)
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 4F comparing ChIP signals at enhancers.

claim: 72.2% of core super-enhancers (363/503) overlap either an intra-TAD loop or a TAD that contains only a single active gene.
source: Strikingly, 72.2% of core super-enhancers (363/503) overlap either an intra-TAD loop or a TAD that contains only a single active gene (defined as a gene expressed at FPKM ≥1 and with a promoter-DHS within 5 kb of the TSS; Supplementary file 1B and Supplementary file 2B)
evidence: This claim describes the overlap between super-enhancers and intra-TAD loops.

claim: Gene targets within an intra-TAD loop are significantly more highly expressed than alternative, linearly more proximal, gene targets outside the loop.
source: Indeed, we found that genes neighboring super-enhancers and found within the same intra-TAD loop are significantly more highly expressed than the alternative potential gene targets, located outside of the intra-TAD loop (Figure 5A).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 5A comparing gene expression inside vs outside loops.

claim: Groups of genes within intra-TAD loops are more uniformly tissue specific or tissue ubiquitous compared to random clusters of genes.
source: Thus, groups of genes within intra-TAD loops are more uniformly tissue specific (as in the case of some super-enhancer-adjacent genes) or tissue ubiquitous (as in the case of groups of housekeeping genes).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 5B comparing variance in Tau scores.

claim: 40% of Alb promoter interactions are localized within DHS that are constituent enhancers of the Alb region super-enhancer.
source: 40% of the interactions are localized within DHS that are constituent enhancers of the Alb region super-enhancer.
evidence: This claim is supported by 4C-seq data analyzing Alb promoter interactions.

claim: >80% of Alb promoter chromatin contacts are within the Alb super-enhancer, and >98% are contained within the Alb intra-TAD loop in both male and female liver.
source: Furthermore, >80% of chromatin contacts are within the Alb super-enhancer, and >98% are contained within the Alb intra-TAD loop, in both male and female liver.
evidence: This claim is supported by 4C-seq data shown in Figure 6A.

claim: 92.9% of male Alb promoter interactions are also present in female liver.
source: Comparing the combined interaction profiles between male and female livers, we observed highly reproducible results, with 92.9% of male interactions also present in female liver (Figure 6—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1C comparing male and female 4C profiles.

claim: >80% of distal high interacting TADs with the Alb promoter are active TADs, and >90% are either active or weakly active TADs.
source: Indeed, we found that >80% of the distal high interacting TADs (both far-cis and trans) were active TADs, and >90% were either active or weakly active TADs.
evidence: This claim is supported by 4C-seq data analyzing distal interactions shown in Figure 6D.

claim: Only 16.6% of non-interacting TADs in cis and 25.9% in trans are active TADs.
source: In contrast, only 16.6% of the non-interacting TADs in cis and 25.9% of those in trans were active TADs (Figure 6B,D).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 6B and 6D comparing TAD activity.

claim: ~90% of DNA loops are associated with both CTCF binding and cohesin binding.
source: First, ~90% of DNA loops ('loop domains', defined as local peaks in the Hi-C contact matrix) are associated with both CTCF binding and cohesin binding, and 92% of such loops involve inwardly oriented CTCF anchors (Rao et al., 2014).
evidence: This is established knowledge from prior high-resolution Hi-C studies, supported by citation.

claim: 92% of CTCF/cohesin-associated loops involve inwardly oriented CTCF anchors.
source: First, ~90% of DNA loops ('loop domains', defined as local peaks in the Hi-C contact matrix) are associated with both CTCF binding and cohesin binding, and 92% of such loops involve inwardly oriented CTCF anchors (Rao et al., 2014).
evidence: This is established knowledge from prior high-resolution Hi-C studies, supported by citation.

claim: Extreme deep sequencing Hi-C studies identify ~10,000 loops with a median size of 185 kb.
source: Second, extreme deep sequencing Hi-C studies identify a much larger number of shorter loops than previously recognized (~10,000 loops with a median size of 185 kb) (Rao et al., 2014)
evidence: This is established knowledge from prior high-resolution Hi-C studies, supported by citation.

claim: Complete knockout of either CTCF or cohesin is embryonic lethal.
source: Complete knockout of either CTCF or cohesin is embryonic lethal (Heath et al., 2008; White et al., 2013; Xu et al., 2010)
evidence: This is established knowledge from prior studies, supported by citations.

claim: Complete removal of CTCF or cohesin-related factors leads to a complete loss of virtually all loop structures in a highly dosage-dependent manner.
source: Complete removal of CTCF or cohesin-related factors, achieved using inducible degradation systems, leads to a complete loss of virtually all loop structures in a highly dosage-dependent manner (Nora et al., 2017; Rao et al., 2017; Schwarzer et al., 2017).
evidence: This is established knowledge from prior studies, supported by citations.

claim: Mutations affecting CAC loop anchors are frequently seen in cancer and lead to dysregulation of adjacent genes.
source: Mutations affecting CAC loop anchors are frequently seen in cancer and lead to dysregulation of adjacent genes, evidencing the functionality of these loops (Ji et al., 2016; Katainen et al., 2015; Fujimoto et al., 2016).
evidence: This is established knowledge from prior studies, supported by citations.
